extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists and policymakers interested in Australian censorship, media law and internet regulation
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive encyclopedia article describing the legal, regulatory and extra-legal forms of censorship in Australia across media, books, film, internet, advertising, universities and national-security contexts. Covers statutes, case law, classification rules, enforcement mechanisms and notable incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied freedom of political communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The Australian Constitution implies a freedom of political communication (recognised in Australian Capital Television Pty Ltd v Commonwealth and Lange v Australian Broadcasting Corporation) that protects political free speech from government prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not a broad free-speech clause: it protects political communication as an essential element of representative government, functions as a shield against government (criminal) prosecution rather than against private civil actions, and is a boundary testable by courts. Not all political speech is necessarily protected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminalisation and limits on political speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite the implied freedom, several laws criminalise forms of speech that might be protected elsewhere (examples: expansion of sedition law post-9/11; historical prosecution of Albert Langer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and governments may still enact or enforce laws (e.g., sedition, electoral laws) that limit speech; the existence of the implied freedom does not guarantee immunity from prosecution in all contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Australian Classification Board refusal criteria (films/books/video games)
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials are generally refused classification because of explicit violent or sexual content, and refused-classification effectively bans sale in Australia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Guidelines state 'adults should be able to read, hear and see what they want', in practice books/films/games may be refused classification for sexual violence, explicit sexual content, extreme violence, or other material that offends standards. Examples: The Peaceful Pill Handbook (RC); prohibitions on depictions of certain sexual fetishes implemented in 2000.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on depictions of persons appearing under 18
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexually explicit depictions of adults who appeared to look under 18 years of age are prohibited by the Classification Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board uses a person's overall appearance to determine whether someone appears to look under 18, and such depictions lead to restriction or refusal of classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Australian Border Force importation standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Imports that 'describe, depict, express or otherwise deal with matters of sex, drug misuse or addiction, crime, cruelty, violence, terrorist acts or revolting or abhorrent phenomena in such a way that they offend against the standards of morality, decency and propriety generally accepted by reasonable adults are not allowed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an operational test used by Border Force to prohibit physical importation of books, films and other goods. The phrasing centres on offence to 'reasonable adults' and broad concepts of morality/decency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refused classification as a legal ban
rubrics_metrics.description: Items rated RC (refused classification) are effectively banned from sale, importation and distribution in Australia under the National Classification Code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include The Anarchist Cookbook (refused 1985) and later editions of The Peaceful Pill Handbook; refusal can be applied to instructional materials that 'promote, incite or instruct in matters of crime or violence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Press freedom factors and measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments (Freedom House, Reporters Without Borders) evaluate press freedom in Australia, noting influences such as judicial suppression orders, police raids, defamation law and media ownership concentration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rankings (e.g., Press Freedom Index) reflect both legal constraints (suppression orders, defamation, RDA) and practical pressures (raids, corporate ties to political leaders). Notable incidents (AFP raids on ABC, raids on journalists) negatively affect assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: National security as a basis for media action
rubrics_metrics.description: The government has acted against media outlets for national security reasons (e.g., police raids seeking evidence of leaks), which can restrict reporting and lead to reviews and criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National-security justifications have been used to seize documents and investigate journalists; such actions are contested by legal, media and civil-liberties groups and feed into debates about press freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression and non-publication orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonwealth, state and territory law allows suppression or non-publication of certain information regarding legal proceedings to avoid jury contamination or protect identities (children, sexual-assault victims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These court orders can ban reporting on matters even when foreign media report them; breaching suppression orders can result in charges (example: charges relating to Cardinal George Pell reporting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation law framework and defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniform defamation laws (since 2006) abolished the libel/slander distinction, introduced defenses (including triviality and truth as an unqualified defense), and restricted corporations' ability to sue for defamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth remains a defense but defendants must show defamatory imputations are substantially true; defenses may be negated by proof of malice; reforms also allowed triviality as a defense and altered corporate standing—practical effect: defamation law is a significant constraint on media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Racial Discrimination Act enforcement against publications
rubrics_metrics.description: The Racial Discrimination Act 1975 has been used to challenge media publications (example: Andrew Bolt found to have contravened the RDA for blog posts deemed discriminatory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RDA complaints can result in legal action against journalists and columnists; proposals to amend the RDA have been politically contentious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising bans and restrictions (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonwealth and State governments ban or restrict certain types of advertising to protect election integrity, regulate personal injury law advertising, and regulate pharmaceutical advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrictions vary by jurisdiction and policy aim (e.g., elections, consumer protection, public health). Enforcement mechanisms and permitted content differ across states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal injury lawyer advertising censorship (Queensland specifics)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Queensland, television and radio advertising by personal injury lawyers is banned and printed/online lawyer statements on personal injury compensation are limited to specific permitted content: lawyer's name/contact/area (print), information on negligence and rights (websites), and terms of service (websites).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provisions were aimed at curbing sensationalist 'cash for injuries' ads. The Queensland government has taken an ultra-strict interpretation, including restrictions on website content, photos, testimonials, case histories and mention of 'personal injury'. Judicial interpretation remained unsettled at the time of the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal injury advertising law in New South Wales
rubrics_metrics.description: New South Wales historically banned all public statements by lawyers concerning personal injury compensation (including websites) with strict penalties; the High Court upheld the law as valid against an argument it infringed implied political communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NSW law was subject to litigation (APLA v Legal Services Commissioner etc.); parts of the regulation were later held void in separate proceedings, and the area remains legally contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: ACMA online material classification review powers
rubrics_metrics.description: If ACMA examines online material under film/video guidelines and finds it would be classified X18+, R18+ without adult verification, or refused classification, it may take action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the site is hosted in Australia, ACMA can issue a 'takedown notice' requiring removal; if hosted overseas, the site may be added to a banned-sites list used by ISPs' filtering software.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory internet filtering design (primary vs secondary blacklists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed mandatory internet filtering included two blacklists: a primary blacklist filtering illegal content (mandatory), and a secondary blacklist filtering content unsuitable for children (users could opt out of secondary but not primary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The primary filter would be mandatory (no opt-out), sparking free-speech concerns about scope and definition of 'illegal' and 'unwanted' content; debate led to political and public backlash and proposals being amended or abandoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blocking pirated content under s.115a (Copyright Amendment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation allows courts to order ISPs to block websites that host pirated content (after procedural steps by rights holders); blocking techniques can include DNS hijacking or URL blocking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Federal Court orders to block The Pirate Bay and other torrent sites; rights holders (e.g., Foxtel, Village Roadshow) applied under these provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-government censorship practices (universities, advertisers, campaigns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of censorship can be enacted non-governmentally: university deplatforming and internal disciplinary action (e.g., sacking of academics), advertiser boycotts to pressure broadcasters (Sleeping Giants), and institutional suppression of internal criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These extra-legal pressures affect academic freedom and media content: concerns include demands to avoid controversial speakers, influence from foreign governments on university administrations, and advertiser-driven removal or suppression of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry self-regulation for advertising and media standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for commercial advertising and many media standards are often enforced through industry self-regulation bodies (e.g., Ad Standards) rather than direct government censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-regulation handles complaints and sets codes; however, self-regulation coexists with statutory rules and classification regimes, and can itself be a source of content moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical enforcement variability and selective application
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Australia has broad censorship laws and powers, enforcement has at times been inconsistent or subject to political will; some proposals were abandoned or not enforced (e.g., Conroy's mandatory filtering ultimately not implemented as proposed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes a combination of restrictive laws with 'almost complete lack of interest in enforcement' by agencies at times, illustrating gaps between statutory power and practical enforcement.
